lead: A heat engine takes heat from a hot body, converts part of it into work, and rejects the rest to a cold body. A refrigerator or heat pump runs the same energy flow backwards: work input moves heat from a cold space to a warm space. The three devices share one balance, Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W. Efficiency and coefficient of performance (COP) compare what you want with what you pay. Room air conditioners, kitchen refrigerators and heat-pump water heaters use this balance every day.
prereq: You need: the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements from 3.1, and the steady-flow energy balance from Unit 1.

sections.h3: The energy balance with consistent signs

blocks.text: Take every heat flow and work flow as a positive magnitude, and fix the direction on a sketch. Q<sub>H</sub> is the heat flow at the hot side, Q<sub>C</sub> is the heat flow at the cold side, and W is the work flow. For a heat engine, Q<sub>H</sub> enters from a hot source, W leaves as useful work, and Q<sub>C</sub> leaves to a cold sink. Energy balance gives Q<sub>H</sub> = W + Q<sub>C</sub>. The engine pays Q<sub>H</sub> and receives W; the second law forces Q<sub>C</sub> > 0, so W < Q<sub>H</sub>.

For a refrigerator, the wanted result is Q<sub>C</sub> removed from a cold space. Work W enters through a compressor, and Q<sub>H</sub> leaves to the kitchen or outdoor air. The balance is Q<sub>C</sub> + W = Q<sub>H</sub>, the same equation. A heat pump is the same hardware with the wanted result changed to Q<sub>H</sub> delivered to a warm space. Some syllabi call a heat pump a reversed heat engine; the phrase means the arrows of heat flow are reversed by work input, not that the device is a different machine. Keep the magnitudes positive in all three cases. The sketch below uses the worked example: 5 kW enters from the cold space, 2 kW of compressor work enters, and 7 kW leaves to the warm space.
A heat engine converts heat into work. Its thermal efficiency η is the work you get divided by the heat you pay for.

blocks.where: η is thermal efficiency (dimensionless); W is net work output; Q<sub>H</sub> is heat taken from the hot source; Q<sub>C</sub> is heat rejected to the cold sink; W, Q<sub>H</sub> and Q<sub>C</sub> use the same unit (kW or MW).

blocks.text: For the engine balance QH = W + QC, so W = QH − QC. Substitute: η = (QH − QC)/QH = 1 − QC/QH. The second law says QC cannot be zero for a cyclic engine that takes heat from one hot source, so η < 1. A steam power plant is a heat engine: fuel or nuclear heat enters the boiler, work leaves at the turbine shaft, and waste heat leaves at the condenser, as in 3.8. Do not insert Celsius temperatures into η. The ratio QC/QH comes from the actual cycle; for a reversible cycle between two reservoirs, the Carnot result links it to Kelvin temperatures, covered in 3.3.
A refrigerator is rated by its coefficient of performance, COP<sub>R</sub>, defined as heat removed from the cold space divided by work input.

blocks.where: COP<sub>R</sub> is the refrigerator coefficient of performance (dimensionless); Q<sub>C</sub> is heat removed from the cold space; W is work input; both in kW or both in MW.

blocks.text: A heat pump is rated by COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/W, because the wanted output is heat delivered to the warm space. Both COPs are dimensionless and both can be greater than 1. A room air conditioner is a refrigerator: it removes Q<sub>C</sub> from the room and rejects Q<sub>H</sub> to the outdoor air. A domestic refrigerator does the same and rejects Q<sub>H</sub> to the kitchen. A heat pump for space heating or hot water wants Q<sub>H</sub>, so it uses the same cycle but a different rating. Divide the balance Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W by W.

blocks.where: COP<sub>HP</sub> is the heat-pump coefficient of performance; Q<sub>H</sub> is heat delivered to the warm space; W is work input.

blocks.text: The difference of 1 is not a small correction; it follows from energy conservation alone. If a refrigerator has COP<sub>R</sub> = 2.5, the same cycle used as a heat pump has COP<sub>HP</sub> = 3.5. That is why a heat pump can deliver more heat than the electrical work it consumes.

figure.caption: The cold space gives 5 kW; the compressor adds 2 kW; the warm space receives 7 kW. Notice that Q<sub>H</sub> is the sum, not the difference.

spec.title: Refrigerator or heat pump
spec.aria: A refrigerator or heat pump takes 5 kW from a 4 °C cold space, receives 2 kW of compressor work, and delivers 7 kW to a 32 °C warm space.

examples.question: A refrigerator removes 5 kW of heat from a cold space at 4 °C and rejects heat to a kitchen at 32 °C. Its compressor draws 2 kW of electrical power. Find the heat rejected to the kitchen, Q<sub>H</sub>, and the coefficient of performance, COP<sub>R</sub>.
steps: Take the refrigerator as the system at steady state. All heat and work magnitudes are positive: Q<sub>C</sub> = 5 kW into the device, W = 2 kW into the device, and Q<sub>H</sub> leaves to the kitchen.
Apply the energy balance: Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W = 5 kW + 2 kW = 7 kW.
Apply the definition: COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/W = 5 kW / 2 kW = 2.5.
examples.answer: The refrigerator rejects Q<sub>H</sub> = 7 kW to the kitchen, and its COP<sub>R</sub> is 2.5.
examples.check:
q_c = 5.0
w = 2.0
q_h = q_c + w
cop_r = q_c / w
print(q_h)
print(cop_r)

traps: Do not swap Q<sub>H</sub> and Q<sub>C</sub>: Q<sub>H</sub> is the larger heat flow to the hot side, Q<sub>C</sub> is the smaller flow from the cold side, and W is their difference.
COP is not W/Q<sub>C</sub>. It is Q<sub>C</sub>/W for a refrigerator and Q<sub>H</sub>/W for a heat pump.
For a refrigerator or heat pump, work input W is positive in the magnitude balance Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W. Do not enter it as negative and then add signs again.
A heat pump and a refrigerator are the same device with a different wanted output; COP<sub>HP</sub> = COP<sub>R</sub> + 1, not a separate cycle.
Do not use Celsius temperatures in η or COP. These are ratios of energies; Celsius enters only through temperature limits such as the Carnot limit in 3.3.

quiz.q: Define a heat engine in one sentence. Which energy flow is the desired output?
quiz.a: A heat engine is a device that takes heat Q<sub>H</sub> from a hot body, converts part of it into work W, and rejects the rest Q<sub>C</sub> to a cold body. The desired output is work W.

quiz.q: Why can a refrigerator have COP<sub>R</sub> greater than 1, while a heat engine cannot have η greater than 1?
quiz.a: They compare different things. COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/W compares heat removed with work paid; a small work input can move a larger amount of heat. η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> compares work produced with heat paid, and the second law forces some Q<sub>C</sub> > 0, so W < Q<sub>H</sub> and η < 1.

quiz.q: A heat pump supplies 12 kW of heat to a room and its compressor draws 4 kW. Find Q<sub>C</sub> removed from outdoors and COP<sub>HP</sub>.
quiz.a: Q<sub>C</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub> − W = 12 kW − 4 kW = 8 kW. COP<sub>HP</sub> = Q<sub>H</sub>/W = 12/4 = 3.

quiz.q: A heat engine receives 10 MW from a furnace and rejects 6 MW to a river. Find W and η.
quiz.a: W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub> = 10 MW − 6 MW = 4 MW. η = W/Q<sub>H</sub> = 4/10 = 0.40, or 40%.

quiz.q: A device moves 5 kW from a cold space and rejects 7 kW to a warm space. Is it a refrigerator or a heat pump? Find both COPs.
quiz.a: W = Q<sub>H</sub> − Q<sub>C</sub> = 7 kW − 5 kW = 2 kW. As a refrigerator, COP<sub>R</sub> = 5/2 = 2.5. As a heat pump, COP<sub>HP</sub> = 7/2 = 3.5. The name depends on the wanted output; the hardware is the same.

quiz.q: A student writes COP<sub>R</sub> = W/Q<sub>C</sub> = 2/5 = 0.4 for the worked example. Identify the error and give the correct value.
quiz.a: COP is wanted output divided by paid input. For a refrigerator the wanted output is Q<sub>C</sub> and the paid input is W, so COP<sub>R</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub>/W = 5/2 = 2.5, not W/Q<sub>C</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does the back of a domestic refrigerator feel warm?
quiz.a: The refrigerator rejects Q<sub>H</sub> = Q<sub>C</sub> + W to the kitchen air. The coils carry this larger heat flow to the surroundings, so they feel warm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real heat pumps are rated by COP at standard test conditions, and the value falls as the outdoor temperature drops. Cascade and absorption systems use the same balances but different work inputs. Search for vapour-compression cycle, seasonal COP and heat pump water heater.
